fields.expected: Most of my recent work has been about the same thing Sierra is doing: making agents that touch real users and real workflows behave reliably. I built a Playwright-based job-application agent in TypeScript where every application moves through an explicit state machine and every mutating capability sits behind fail-closed flags like SUBMIT_ENABLED. Free-text and demographic fields are architecturally blocked from auto-fill and always generate a human-review item. Workday and iCIMS are detected and skipped rather than handled unreliably. I made those choices because a single wrong browser action submits a real application, and I care as much about where automation should stop as where it can go. At Intelehealth I built an evaluation framework comparing LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard using stratified sampling to surface systematic failure modes, which convinced me that judging whether an output should be trusted is the harder problem. That is why Sierra interests me specifically: you are shipping agents to companies like Uber and Sutter Health, where a wrong answer has consequences, so craftsmanship and evaluation are not optional. I want to own real pieces of a system like that.

fields.expected:
The best agent engineers I can imagine are as careful about where an agent should stop as they are about what it can do, and they treat evaluation as a real engineering problem rather than a spot check. Building the job-application agent forced both on me. I designed a validation ladder, UNIT_CONFIRMED to FIXTURE_CONFIRMED to LIVE_READ_ONLY_CONFIRMED to LIVE_MUTATION_CONFIRMED, because a capability passing against a local fixture does not mean it works against a live Greenhouse form. I also skipped Workday, iCIMS, and Oracle entirely rather than handling them unreliably, which I think is the right instinct when a wrong action submits a real application.

The second quality is caring whether the output is actually usable by a person. At Intelehealth I built an evaluation framework for AI-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard, using stratified sampling to surface systematic failure modes rather than average scores. On the anomaly-detection system I work on now, I built a learning-to-rank layer and a retrieval-augmented explanation layer, because a detector that fires constantly just creates a second problem.

I also ship. ClarityAtlas went into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users.

fields.expected: Two things that don't fit neatly into the other answers. First, a lot of what I do outside coursework is getting things in front of people. With ClarityAtlas, the iOS health product I lead technically, building the passive sleep-estimation system from HealthKit and Core Motion signals was only half the work. The other half was recruiting users into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users, getting into NSF I-Corps and the Pava Spark Accelerator, and, at one point, knocking on the doors of Garland Hall until we got to pitch President Daniels, which eventually turned into a formal meeting. I like work where shipping and convincing people are both part of the job. Second, I've spent the past year independently studying how research gets funded and evaluated, talking with researchers, administrators, and science-policy people, and I keep landing on the same question: as AI makes generation cheap, judgment becomes the scarce thing. That's why agent reliability interests me as a technical problem and not just a safety checkbox. I'm an undergrad (Applied Math and Statistics, Economics, class of 2029), and I learn fastest by owning something real.
